notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 1 Kings 21, compiled from the sources I was able to access.

---

## 1 Kings 21 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: *"Some time later, Naboth the Jezreelite happened to own a vineyard in Jezreel next to the palace of Ahab king of Samaria."*

This opening sets the scene "after these things" — that is, after Ahab's two victories over Ben-hadad of Syria and his wrongful release of that blaspheming king (ch. 20). The phrase signals a moral downturn: God had just given Ahab victory, and now Ahab uses his security to covet a neighbor's land (Gill). Naboth is identified as a Jezreelite. There is a textual and geographical difficulty: some manuscripts (LXX) place the vineyard in Samaria near the threshing-floor of Ahab, not in Jezreel; the Vulgate reads "who was in Jezreel" (referring to Naboth, not the vineyard). Ellicott suggests the vineyard may have been an outlying property near Samaria, though Naboth's ancestral "plot of ground" (2 Kings 9:25–26) was certainly at Jezreel. Constable, following Napier, holds the vineyard was in Jezreel — Ahab's winter capital.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### v. 2: *"So Ahab said to Naboth, 'Give me your vineyard to use as a vegetable garden, since it is next to my palace. I will give you a better vineyard in its place—or if you prefer, I will give you its value in silver.'"*

Ahab's offer was, on its face, courteous and reasonable — a trade or cash purchase, not an outright seizure (Gill, Ellicott, Guzik). Gill notes Ahab may have been influenced by Syrian gardening customs (herb gardens near palaces). Guzik describes it as "a simple attempted real estate transaction." Yet the seemingly innocent request masks covetousness: a king who could have anything grew fixated on the one plot he could not lawfully have. Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik) remarks: "He was lord over ten-twelfths of the land, and became miserable because he could not get a poor man's vineyard."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html

### v. 3: *"But Naboth replied, 'The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.'"*

Naboth's refusal was not stubbornness but obedience to the Mosaic Law. Leviticus 25:23 forbade permanent sale of ancestral land; Numbers 36:7 prohibited transfer of inheritance between tribes. Land in Israel belonged ultimately to the LORD, parceled out as a sacred trust (Guzik, Constable, Gill). Guzik notes that real estate in ancient Israel "was never really sold, only leased — and that only under the most dire circumstances." Gill adds that Naboth was a conscientious man, likely one of the 7,000 who had not bowed to Baal. Ellicott observes that Naboth's reply has "a certain tone of harshness, perhaps of unnecessary discourtesy, implying condemnation, as well as rejection, of the offer of the king" — yet Naboth was legally and morally right.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### v. 4: *"So Ahab went to his palace, sullen and angry because Naboth the Jezreelite had told him, 'I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers.' He lay down on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat."*

Ahab's response reveals his character: weak, petulant, and childish. Ellicott compares him to "a spoilt child" who throws himself on his bed and refuses food — and to Haman in Esther 5:13, for whom all was worthless because of one man. Guzik calls him "a spineless, pouting man." Constable notes that the Hebrew words for "sullen and vexed" (also used in 1 Kings 20:43) reflect Ahab's perception that Naboth's legal position was unassailable. John Piper (Desiring God) observes: Ahab "crumbles into self-pity and passivity" — a dangerous posture that leaves room for a more ruthless partner to act. The Precept Austin summary quotes Alexander Maclaren, who identifies Ahab as "wicked and weak."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-perils-of-a-passive-man
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### v. 5: *"Soon his wife Jezebel came in and asked, 'Why are you so sullen that you refuse to eat?'"*

Jezebel notices her husband's mood. Gill says she perceived he was low-spirited and wanted to relieve him — but her method of "relief" would be murder. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Ahab's sullen refusal to eat was the "natural seedplot of crime, under the instigation of more determined wickedness" (from the search excerpt).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-21.html (via search excerpt)

### v. 6: *"Ahab answered, 'Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and told him, "Give me your vineyard for silver, or if you wish, I will give you another vineyard in its place." And he replied, "I will not give you my vineyard!"'"*

Ahab's report to Jezebel is subtly dishonest: he omits Naboth's theological reason ("the inheritance of my fathers") and makes Naboth sound merely obstinate and surly (Gill). He also omits that he offered a trade, presenting himself as the reasonable party rebuffed. This selective retelling is characteristic of self-pity: Ahab casts himself as victim.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html

### v. 7: *"But his wife Jezebel said to him, 'Do you not reign over Israel? Get up, eat some food, and be cheerful, for I will get you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.'"*

Jezebel's question is biting irony: "Do you now govern Israel?" — meaning, "You call yourself king but let a subject cross your will?" (Ellicott). Constable identifies the theological root of the problem: Jezebel (and Ahab, cf. 1 Kings 20:42) believed the king was the supreme authority in Israel, failing to acknowledge Yahweh's sovereignty. Ellicott compares her to Lady Macbeth — half-contemptuous of her husband's weakness, ready to act where he only desires. Guzik notes her speech "revealed who really exercised authority in the palace." She promises the vineyard without money or exchange — she will simply take it.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/

### v. 8: *"Then Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal, and sent them to the elders and nobles who lived with Naboth in his city."*

The seal was the royal signet, engraved on stone and impressed on clay (Ellicott). Its use required Ahab's collusion — he had to know something was being done in his name, even if he avoided inquiring about details (Guzik, Ellicott, Wiseman cited by Guzik). Jezebel wrote "in Ahab's name" — the authority was his, and God would hold him responsible. "His city" most naturally means Jezreel, where Naboth lived (Ellicott).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/

### vv. 9–10: *"In the letters she wrote: 'Proclaim a fast and give Naboth a seat of honor among the people. But seat two scoundrels opposite him and have them testify, "You have cursed both God and the king!" Then take him out and stone him to death.'"*

Jezebel's plot was diabolically clever — and clothed in religious form. A fast suggested some hidden sin bringing divine judgment on the community, requiring a scapegoat to be found (Guzik, Ellicott). Naboth was seated "on high" — probably the place where the accused stood to face trial (Gill). Two "sons of Belial" (worthless, lawless men) were procured as false witnesses, complying with Deuteronomy 17:6–7 which required two witnesses for a capital case (Constable, Ellicott). The charge — cursing God and king — made the crime both religious and political, carrying the death penalty (Leviticus 24:16) and forfeiture of property. Constable notes that Jezebel "elevated cursing the king to a crime on the same level with cursing Yahweh," consistent with her pagan view of kingship. Guzik observes the parallel with Jesus' trial, where false witnesses accused Him of offending both God and Caesar.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html

### vv. 11–13: *"So the elders and nobles who lived in Naboth's city did as Jezebel had instructed … they proclaimed a fast … seated Naboth with high honor … the two scoundrels came in and sat opposite Naboth, and these men testified … 'Naboth has cursed both God and the king!' So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death."*

The ready compliance of the city's leadership is especially damning. Gill expresses shock: "that the elders and nobles … should be so sadly and universally depraved as to execute such a piece of villany, is really surprising." Ellicott calls this "characteristic of the baser forms of organised Eastern despotism — not venturing to take life by simple violence without some cause apparently shown, and yet always able to poison the springs of justice." Alexander Maclaren (cited by Guzik) identifies three dangerous character types: (1) Ahab, wicked and weak; (2) Jezebel, wicked and strong; (3) the elders of Jezreel, wicked and subservient. Naboth was taken outside the city for execution, as the Law prescribed for blasphemers (Leviticus 24:14). 2 Kings 9:26 indicates Naboth's sons were killed with him, eliminating all heirs (Guzik, Constable).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html

### v. 14: *"Then they sent word to Jezebel: 'Naboth has been stoned to death.'"*

The message went to Jezebel, not Ahab — confirming who was truly directing the crime (Gill). The elders knew this would please her.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html

### vv. 15–16: *"When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned to death, she said to Ahab, 'Get up and take possession of the vineyard … For Naboth is no longer alive, but dead.' And when Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to take possession …"*

Jezebel's words are chillingly pragmatic. Gill and Ellicott note that the property of executed traitors would fall to the crown — and with Naboth's sons also dead (2 Kings 9:26), there were no heirs. Ahab's response is telling: he asks no questions. As Ellicott puts it, he is "desirous to be innocent of the knowledge, and yet tacitly to applaud the deed." Guzik calls this "evil added to evil." The LXX contains a curious interpolation at this point: "he rent his clothes and put on sackcloth" — suggesting Ahab felt momentary horror before proceeding anyway (Ellicott). Constable observes Ahab "did not reprove her but took advantage of her actions and in doing so approved them." G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik): "Ahab never possessed the vineyard of Naboth. He held it, but that very fact became to him a torment."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### vv. 17–18: *"Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, 'Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria. See, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, of which he has gone to take possession.'"*

Elijah re-emerges after a long silence (since the call of Elisha in ch. 19). Ellicott notes he took no part in the political events of chapter 20 but "emerges now for the higher moral duty of rebuking crime and avenging innocent blood." The phrase "who is in Samaria" is taken by Ellicott literally — Ahab was in Samaria, not Jezreel, when the word came. Constable sees it as an ironical reference to Ahab's capital. God's timing is precise: Ahab goes to claim his ill-gotten prize and runs straight into the prophet of God (Guzik). Gill notes that Elijah had likely been occupied training prophets in the schools during his absence from the narrative.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html

### v. 19: *"Tell him that this is what the LORD says: 'Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?' Then tell him that this is also what the LORD says: 'In the place where the dogs licked up the blood of Naboth, there also the dogs will lick up your blood—yes, yours!'"*

Elijah's accusation is stunning in its brevity and directness: murder and theft — two violations of the Ten Commandments — pinned squarely on Ahab, not Jezebel. God held Ahab responsible as husband, king, and beneficiary (Guzik, Constable). Ellicott calls it "stern, indignant brevity … shaming the subterfuge by which Ahab shifts his guilt to Jezebel." The prophecy about the dogs licking Ahab's blood "in the place where dogs licked Naboth's blood" presents a difficulty, since Ahab died in Samaria (1 Kings 22:38) and his blood was washed from his chariot at the pool of Samaria, not in Jezreel. Multiple solutions are proposed: (a) Guzik and Constable argue the judgment was transferred to Ahab's son Joram, whose blood was shed on Naboth's plot (2 Kings 9:25–26), in light of v. 29; (b) Ellicott insists the personal sentence was *not* deferred — only the dynastic one — and that the prophecy was literally fulfilled at the pool of Samaria (1 Kings 22:38), reading "in the place where" as "because" or "inasmuch as." Gill and older commentators sometimes read the Hebrew *bimqom asher* causally: "because dogs have licked …" (Junius, Tremellius, Grotius).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### v. 20: *"When Elijah arrived, Ahab said to him, 'So you have found me out, my enemy.' He replied, 'I have found you out because you have sold yourself to do evil in the sight of the LORD.'"*

Ahab's greeting is "partly of dismay, partly of excuse" (Ellicott). He attempts to frame Elijah's confrontation as personal enmity, just as in 1 Kings 18:17 he called Elijah "the troubler of Israel." Elijah's reply cuts through: he is not an enemy by choice — Ahab has made himself God's enemy by "selling himself" to evil. The Pulpit Commentary explains "sold thyself" means surrendering oneself wholly as a slave to sin (cf. Romans 7:14). Constable notes the Hebrew wordplay: Ahab sold himself to do *ra‘* (evil); God will bring *ra‘ah* (calamity/disaster) on him. F.B. Meyer (quoted by Guzik): "Though the king knew it not, Elijah was his best friend; Jezebel his direst foe."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### vv. 21–22: *"This is what the LORD says: 'I will bring calamity on you and consume your descendants; I will cut off from Ahab every male in Israel, both slave and free. I will make your house like that of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like that of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have provoked My anger and caused Israel to sin.'"*

This is the dynastic doom: the house of Omri will be exterminated just as Jeroboam's and Baasha's dynasties were (1 Kings 15:29; 16:11–12). Ellicott distinguishes this from the personal judgment of v. 19: it is this dynastic sentence, not the personal one, that is deferred by Ahab's repentance (v. 29). The phrase "him that pisseth against the wall" (KJV) is a crude Hebrew idiom for every male. Constable notes the wordplay between "evil" (v. 20) and "calamity/disaster" (v. 21), emphasizing the correspondence between sin and punishment.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### v. 23: *"And the LORD also speaks concerning Jezebel: 'The dogs will devour Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.'"*

Elijah has not named Jezebel until now, leaving Ahab fully exposed as the responsible party. Now he pronounces her fate: her body will be thrown outside the city wall into the "ditch" (margin) where scavenger dogs feed on refuse — a death of utter dishonor (Ellicott). This prophecy was fulfilled exactly in 2 Kings 9:30–37. Constable notes there is no hint Jezebel ever repented.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html

### v. 24: *"Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city will be eaten by dogs, and anyone who dies in the field will be eaten by the birds of the air."*

This formula echoes 1 Kings 14:11 and 16:4 — the standard pronouncement of dynastic extermination with dishonorable death (no burial). Gill notes this concludes the words of the Lord through Elijah; vv. 25–26 are the historian's editorial comment.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html

### vv. 25–26: *"(Surely there was never one like Ahab, who sold himself to do evil in the sight of the LORD, incited by his wife Jezebel. He committed the most detestable acts by going after idols, just like the Amorites whom the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.)"*

These verses are the inspired narrator's assessment. Ahab was uniquely wicked — "none like Ahab" — not only because of the Naboth crime but because of the entire pattern of idolatry and apostasy. Guzik notes the parallel to Genesis 3:17 ("because you have heeded the voice of your wife") — God holds husbands who follow their wives into sin to special account. Constable observes: "He was as bad as the Canaanites whom God drove out because of their wickedness" — preparing the theological ground for Israel's own future exile. The comparison to the Amorites is especially pointed: Israel was supposed to displace Canaanite wickedness, not replicate it.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### v. 27: *"When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and fasted. He lay down in sackcloth and walked around meekly."*

Ahab's response was outwardly exactly right: tearing garments, sackcloth on bare flesh, fasting, and walking softly (or barefoot, as the Targum and Josephus suggest — Ellicott, Gill). The Pulpit Commentary says "all these were signs of contrition and humiliation." Yet most commentators agree the repentance was external and superficial. Poole (cited by Guzik): "this humiliation or repentance of Ahab's was only external and superficial, arising from the terror of God's judgments; and not sincere and serious … as appears, because … there is not the least intimation of any one sign or fruit of his true repentance, as that he restored Naboth's land, or reproved his infamous wife." Guzik adds: "Three years later, Ahab was dead under God's judgment." Constable however calls it "genuine repentance," noting that God Himself accepts it as such in the next verse. John Piper (Desiring God) calls it a striking moment: "The selfish, prideful, passive husband became a humble one, at least for a time."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-perils-of-a-passive-man
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html

### vv. 28–29: *"Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: 'Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me? Because he has humbled himself before Me, I will not bring the calamity during his days, but I will bring it upon his house in the days of his son.'"*

This is one of the most remarkable displays of divine mercy in the Old Testament. God Himself draws Elijah's attention to Ahab's humbling and responds with mitigated judgment. The Pulpit Commentary: "The repentance, if it was not profound, or enduring, was nevertheless, while it lasted, sincere. The Searcher of hearts saw in it a genuine self-abasement. And 'He will not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax'" (Isaiah 42:3). Ellicott adds: "Man's judgment would despise it; God sees in its imperfection some germs of promise." Several points are debated:

- **Baptist/Reformed (Gill)**: Records a Jewish tradition that Ahab's repentance was true and his conversion thorough, but Gill himself rejects this: "we never read that he reproved Jezebel … nor restored the vineyard … nor did he leave his idols." Yet Gill also notes that Luther "from these words concluded, and was persuaded, that he was saved."

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik)**: Emphasizes the power of even shallow repentance to move God's heart: "The worst sinner should not disqualify himself from receiving God's mercy." God "honored Ahab's initiative" — showing that prophetic judgment is always an invitation to repentance.

- **Anglican (Ellicott)**: Distinguishes the personal sentence (which was *not* deferred — Ahab still died violently) from the dynastic sentence (which *was* deferred to Jehoram's day). Ahab would "die in honour" on the battlefield, and the full destruction would wait until Jehoram filled up the measure of iniquity.

- **Evangelical (Constable)**: Notes the parallel to Exodus 32:14 and Jeremiah 18:6–12 — God relents when sinners repent. "Not Ahab but his son Joram would bleed on Naboth's land in Jezreel."

- **Reformed Baptist (Piper via Desiring God)**: Calls God's response "a startling mercy nonetheless. Disaster is not averted for the dynasty, but it is for Ahab. How ready is our God to show mercy, even for one who gave himself to evil like no other?"

The Pulpit Commentary also addresses the apparent injustice of punishing the son: "There is no injustice here … if the son had departed from his father's sins he would have been spared (Ezekiel 18:14ff.); the sentence would have been revoked. Judgment was deferred to give the house of Ahab another chance."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-21.html
- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-perils-of-a-passive-man
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-21.html (Pulpit, from search excerpt)

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**The nature of Ahab's repentance (v. 27–29)** is the main point of divergence:

- **Reformed / Baptist (Gill, Poole)**: Ahab's repentance was external, temporary, and merely from fear of punishment — not true saving repentance. Evidence: he never restored the land, rebuked Jezebel, or abandoned idols; in the very next chapter he consults false prophets. The mercy shown was temporal only (deferring earthly judgment), not salvific.

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Guzik)**: While also skeptical of Ahab's sincerity ("shallow," "external and superficial"), Guzik draws a strong application about God's readiness to respond even to imperfect repentance — a pastoral point that God "opened the door of mercy."

- **Lutheran (Luther, cited by Gill)**: Luther apparently concluded from these verses that Ahab was saved — a striking instance of the Lutheran emphasis on grace alone. (I could not access lcms.org or 1517.org to verify current Lutheran teaching due to search limits.)

- **Reformed Baptist (Piper / Desiring God)**: Holds the tension: Ahab's humbling was genuine *as far as it went* (God Himself attests to it), and God's mercy in response is startling and real, though temporal and limited.

**The fulfillment of the blood prophecy (v. 19)**:

- **Guzik, Constable**: The prophecy was transferred to Ahab's son Joram (2 Kings 9:25–26) because of v. 29.
- **Ellicott**: Insists the personal prophecy *was* fulfilled literally at the pool of Samaria (1 Kings 22:38) and that only the *dynastic* judgment was deferred by v. 29. Ellicott reads "in the place where" emphatically and literally.
- **Gill, older commentators**: Some read the Hebrew preposition causally — "because dogs licked" rather than "in the place where dogs licked."
